system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-12-11 11:56:00 to 2187-12-19 12:52:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with inoperable cholangiocarcinoma and a history of recurrent biliary infections, was admitted for fever (101.3°F) following a routine percutaneous biliary drain (PTBD) exchange. He was afebrile upon arrival and remained so throughout hospitalization. Initial labs showed mild pancytopenia, which stabilized, and liver enzymes were within baseline. Blood cultures remained negative, and ultrasound showed no new biliary obstruction or abscess. The fever was attributed to transient bacteremia post-procedure. Constipation with tarry stools was noted, but no acute gastrointestinal bleed was evident. He was managed with a short course of IV meropenem, then transitioned back to home suppressive Bactrim. Apixaban was held due to prior thrombocytopenia, with recommendation to discuss restart with oncology. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up planned.
problems: Benign prostatic hyperplasia without lower urinary tract symptoms
Migraine, unspecified, not intractable, without status migrainosus

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with fevers, r/o PNA  // rule out PNA

EXAMINATION:  CT ABD AND PELVIS WITH CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with fevers chills PTBD  // any abscess/intra
abdominal evidence of infection to explain high fevers/chills; is PTBD in
place?

TECHNIQUE:  Single phase contrast: MDCT axial images were acquired through the
abdomen and pelvis following intravenous contrast administration.
Oral contrast was not administered.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.

DOSE:  Acquisition sequence:
   1) Stationary Acquisition 6.0 s, 0.5 cm; CTDIvol = 28.9 mGy (Body) DLP =
14.4 mGy-cm.
   2) Spiral Acquisition 6.4 s, 50.6 cm; CTDIvol = 14.3 mGy (Body) DLP = 723.1
mGy-cm.
 Total DLP (Body) = 738 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior CTs of the abdomen pelvis, most recent dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: Aside from mild dependent atelectasis bilaterally, the visualized
lung fields are within normal limits.  There is no evidence of pleural or
pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrates homogenous attenuation throughout.  A
percutaneous transhepatic biliary drain is seen in similar position as on
prior CT, with its tip coiled in the duodenum.  Two new rounded, hypodense
lesions with hyperenhancing rim have developed in the right hepatic lobe (2:
32,35).  The subcapsular lesion, has a somewhat scalloped appearance 2:35). 
Mild intrahepatic biliary dilatation persists, and is similar to mildly
increased in comparison to the prior CT.  Left hepatic lobe pneumobilia is
again noted.  No extrahepatic biliary dilatation.  2 biliary stents and a
portal venous stent are in stable position.  The gallbladder is surgically
absent.

PANCREAS: The pancreas is atrophic, with stable pancreatic ductal dilatation,
and 2 small foci of air within the pancreatic duct, measuring up to 3 mm.  On
the previous scan, a solitary focus measuring 5 mm was identified.  There is
no peripancreatic stranding.

SPLEEN: Stable splenomegaly.  The spleen shows normal attenuation throughout. 
Multiple small calcified granulomas are noted.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: The kidneys are of normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram. 
There is a stable 1.6 cm simple cyst in the left lower pole.  A 1.1 x 1.2
superior pole rounded hypodensity in the right kidney, measures 22 Hounsfield
units, previously having measured 36 and may represent a hemorrhagic or
proteinaceous cyst.  Several other bilateral, subcentimeter hypodensities are
too small to characterize however likely represent simple renal cysts.  There
is no  hydronephrosis.  There is no perinephric abnormality.

GASTROINTESTINAL: The stomach is unremarkable.  Small bowel loops demonstrate
normal caliber, wall thickness, and enhancement throughout. Sigmoid
diverticulosis without evidence of diverticulitis without diverticulitis,
otherwise the colon and rectum are within normal limits. The appendix is not
clearly identified.

PELVIS: The urinary bladder and distal ureters are unremarkable.  There is no
free fluid in the pelvis.

REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS: The prostate and seminal vesicles are grossly
unremarkable noting a central defect in the prostate suggestive of prior TURP.

LYMPH NODES: There is no retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  There
is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

VASCULAR: There is no abdominal aortic aneurysm.  Mild atherosclerotic disease
is noted.  No definite evidence of portal vein thrombosis as identified on
prior CT scans.  Splenic and gastric varices are again noted.

BONES: There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or acute fracture. 
Degenerative changes of the lumbar spine.

SOFT TISSUES: The abdominal and pelvic wall is within normal limits.

IMPRESSION:


1. Two new hypodense, right hepatic lobe lesions with peripheral enhancement
is concerning for abscesses or possibly metastatic disease.
2. PTBD in similar position comparison to the prior CT.  Portal venous stent
and 2 biliary stents also appear to be in stable position.
3. Stable to mildly progressed intrahepatic ductal dilatation.  Persistent
pneumobilia, consistent with presence of biliary drains and stents.
4. Stable pancreatic duct dilatation.
5. Stable splenomegaly.

25mcg of fentanyl and 0.5 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service

PROCEDURE:
1. Pull-back cholangiogram through existing right percutaneous transhepatic
biliary drainage access.
2. Exchange of the existing 12 ___ percutaneous transhepatic biliary
drainage catheter with a new 12 ___ internal external PTBD catheter.
3. Ultrasound interrogation of the right hepatic lobe.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:
Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to the
procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the patient. The patient
was then brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the exam table.
A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___ protocol.

After local anesthesia, the existing PTB D was cut and removed over ___
wire.  A 7 ___ sheath was advanced and a pull-back cholangiogram was
performed.  A new 12 ___ internal external PTB D catheter destrung was then
advanced under fluoroscopic guidance with tip in the duodenum.  The catheter
was secured with 0 silk sutures and a StatLock.  A sterile dressing was
applied.
Ultrasound interrogation of the right hepatic lobe was performed with findings
as described below.
The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  Pull-back cholangiogram demonstrated patent right intrahepatic ducts as
well as CBD with flow into the duodenum.  No evidence of filling defects to
suggest blood clots or pus within the bile ducts.
2.  A piece of the indwelling PTB D catheter was sent for culture.
3.  Ultrasound interrogation of the right hepatic lobe failed to demonstrate
the small areas of concern seen on the recent CT scan which could represent
small abscesses.

IMPRESSION: 

Pull-back cholangiogram and ultrasound interrogation of the right hepatic lobe
with findings as described above.  Replacement of a 12 ___ internal
external PTB D catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I've been reviewing why you came in. You had a fever at home yesterday—101.2—and your wife noticed blood from your biliary drain when she uncapped it. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. I felt awful—fever, nausea, and some belly pain. But the pain’s gone now. I was worried about the blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve checked your labs and imaging. Your white count is a bit low, platelets are also low, but your liver enzymes are stable. The CT scan shows your biliary stents are in place, but we did see two new small spots in your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Spots? Are they cancer? I thought I was cancer-free after the radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great question. Your oncologist reviewed the scans and believes these are more likely small abscesses, not cancer. They’re too small to drain, but they could be why you got sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So infection again? I’ve had this so many times. Is it from the drain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because of your anatomy and the biliary drain, you’re at higher risk for infections. We started you on IV meropenem to cover possible bacteria, including resistant ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Bactrim at home. Did I miss a dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You said you vomited yesterday—might have lost the dose. That could’ve lowered your protection. We’ll keep you on strong antibiotics and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the blood from the drain? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. It was bright red but stopped. We don’t think it’s active bleeding. Sometimes the drain irritates the tract. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My knee’s been bothering me too—chronic pain. Capsaicin made it burn, but lidocaine patches help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on the lidocaine patches. We also noticed you’re quite weak—likely from being sick and not moving much. Physical therapy will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired. And I haven’t been sleeping—insomnia’s been terrible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started mirtazapine last night—it helps sleep and anxiety. We’re avoiding benzos because they can worsen confusion, which you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I get confused when I’m sick. And I’ve had thrush—white patches in my mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started nystatin for that. Also, since flu’s going around, we’re giving Tamiflu for 10 days as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. But I trust you. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch your fever, repeat labs, and likely do a procedure to exchange your biliary drain. It might be clogged or not draining well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? It’s so invasive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But it’s important to keep the bile flowing and reduce infection risk. We’ll do it under imaging guidance and with sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative, which is good—no ongoing bloodstream infection. But we did grow some bacteria from your old catheter tip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Gram-negative rods and Enterococcus. That supports we’re on the right antibiotics. The procedure to exchange your drain is scheduled for today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they check if the liver spots are better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The interventional radiologist will do a cholangiogram—inject contrast to see the ducts—and also use ultrasound to look at the liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We exchanged your 12 French PTBD catheter. The cholangiogram showed your ducts are open, bile is flowing into the duodenum—no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the abscesses?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound didn’t see the small areas clearly—could mean they’re resolving. We’ll follow up with your oncologist, but for now, this is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. My energy’s a bit better. Still weak though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Physical therapy saw you this morning. You’re improving. We’re also consulting nutrition—you’ve lost weight and need support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are trending better. White count is up, liver enzymes are stable. Infectious disease recommends switching from meropenem to ertapenem for four weeks at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: IV antibiotics at home? How will that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nurse will come daily to give the infusion through your midline. They’ll also check your labs weekly. ID will see you in clinic to monitor progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? I’m on so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue finasteride, pantoprazole, ursodiol, and your sleep meds. We’re stopping sertraline—mirtazapine is helping your mood and sleep better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Mirtazapine helps anxiety too. We’ll increase it to 15 mg in two weeks if needed. Avoid benzos—they can cloud your thinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No fever in two days. Your drain is draining clear fluid. PT says you can walk independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll arrange home health for the IV antibiotics and check you’re safe to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I miss my routine. And my wife.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge plan is confirmed. You’ll get ertapenem daily for four weeks, lidocaine patches for your knee, nystatin for thrush, and Tamiflu for nine more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Bactrim?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll restart it after the ertapenem course. We don’t want to over-suppress or cause resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor in one week, oncology in two, and infectious disease in three. They’ll decide if you need another liver scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood from the drain—should I panic if it happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s a small amount and stops, monitor. If it’s heavy or you feel dizzy, go to the ER. Otherwise, call your GI team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking mirtazapine and melatonin. Avoid screens at night. We’ll reassess in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check. You’re alert, walking well, no fever, eating normally. We’re confident you can go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so worried this was cancer again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But right now, everything points to infection, not cancer. Your oncologist agrees. Keep up with follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll watch for fever or drain issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call if you have fever, chills, or significant pain. Otherwise, rest and let the antibiotics do their job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. Today’s the day. You’re being discharged. Nurse will go over your meds and supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: daily IV antibiotics, keep the drain site clean, and follow up with all your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Johnson. Wishing you a smooth recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your platelets are still low from chemo, so avoid heavy lifting or injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. No gardening for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart. And keep using the lidocaine patches—they help with pain and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is glad to help. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Rest well and take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with a history of inoperable cholangiocarcinoma and recurrent biliary infections, was admitted for fever (101.2°F) and blood from his percutaneous biliary drain (PTBD). Initial evaluation revealed stable vital signs, mild lab abnormalities, and two new hypodense liver lesions on CT, concerning for microabscesses. Blood cultures were negative, but catheter tip cultures grew gram-negative rods and Enterococcus. He underwent successful exchange of his PTBD catheter, with cholangiogram confirming patent ducts and no obstruction. He was treated with IV meropenem, then transitioned to a four-week course of outpatient ertapenem as recommended by infectious disease. His symptoms improved, delirium resolved, and he was discharged home with home health services for IV antibiotics. Follow-up was arranged with oncology, infectious disease, and primary care to monitor response and consider repeat imaging.
